name: dark-gate-r1
context:
GAME THREE, DARKMATTER, AT ITS VISUAL GATE. You audited two earlier versions of this design and returned REVISE on both. This is the third, built out of the discriminator you named, and it is submitted with its screenshots, its proof, and the defects the screenshots found.

═══════════ WHAT YOU RULED LAST TIME ═══════════

"The next step is the most dangerous: deciding if the player's failure is because they are BLIND (needs a forecast) or because they are CLUMSY (needs continuous control)." And the strongest objection you raised against a forecast: "A forecast cone solves for uncertainty. However, if a 1-degree error in the first shot results in a 180-degree error in the second, a forecast is merely a high-resolution view of your own inevitable failure. A map is not a steering wheel."

That was run, with a third arm your objection demanded -- PERFECT FORESIGHT WITH UNCHANGED HANDS, which bounds what a forecast of any fidelity can buy:

  bearings  served  BLIND  my FORECAST  FORESIGHT  RANDOM  absolute ceiling
        12   14/24  16.3%       12.9%      49.7%   12.8%             0.842
        24   16/24  12.0%        3.7%      43.4%    8.3%             0.837

CLUMSY IS DEAD: doubling the lattice moves the absolute ceiling by -0.5 points and makes every human policy WORSE. Your objection is HALF upheld -- a better steering wheel is worth measurably nothing, and the map is worth +33.4 points. And the gap that mattered was inside the information arms: a forecast made 49.7% available and my rule for using one delivered 12.9%, worse than having no forecast at all.

So the missing thing was never the forecast. IT WAS A RULE FOR READING ONE. Both policies that had failed -- mine and yours -- reason about DIRECTION, which the intuition curve says is knowable (100% correct within 45 degrees at 30 steps, 95.4% at 120, 67.6% at 360, 42.6% at 600), and neither touches MAGNITUDE, which is knowable at no horizon.

═══════════ WHAT WAS BUILT ═══════════

GHOST LANDINGS. The engine already integrates the future for each of the fourteen lattice actions; the interface draws WHERE THE MARKED BODY ENDS UP under each. The player does not read a forecast and infer a magnitude -- they see fourteen dots and a ring and pick the nearest. A nearest-neighbour comparison, rather than a magnitude estimate.

The sentence the whole game reduces to: "Drop a mass, or spin the cluster, to steer the marked body into the ring before your budget runs out." Twelve bearings plus two spin directions, two shots, five bodies, 120 steps per shot, Q32.32 fixed point, bitwise-replayable from the seed.

Measured, 24 seeds, 196 sequences per seed:

  RANDOM (priced)                        11.5% of the ceiling
  BLIND, aim-watch-aim                   16.3%
  YOUR spin-then-aim                     15.2%
  GHOST, pick the nearest dot            78.8%

  move-value entropy                     5.30 bits
  live sequences within 10% of ceiling   3.6 of 196
  agency over doing nothing              0.842

One gate was written TO FAIL IF THE SCORE WENT TOO HIGH -- a mechanic that takes a human to the ceiling has solved the game rather than made it playable, which is the standing objection to every observability mechanic in this project. It passed at <=85%.

═══════════ WHAT THE SCREENSHOT FOUND THAT NO METRIC DID ═══════════

The rules were moved out of the probe into a shipping module and the gate sheet renders one real round end to end. Looking at it found four things, and one of them is a DESIGN defect that the simulation found independently and simultaneously:

  1. THE TRAILS DREW THE FUTURE. The generator ran a clone forward and painted the result as history -- where a body WILL be, in the visual language of where it HAS been.
  2. ALL FIVE PANELS DREW THE SAME STATE. The view object holds a live reference to the universe and the panels were rendered at the end, so every one showed the final frame. "SEEDED" was captioned five bodies at step 80 and rendered seven bodies at step 320.
  3. THE DECISION WAS AN UNREADABLE BLOB, AND FRAMING ON THE BODY MADE IT WORSE. Over a 240-step round the marked body DRIFTS much further than the landings SPREAD, so including its position in the camera extent hands the scale to the drift and collapses the whole choice into a few pixels. The frame is now the ghosts and the ring, and the body is usually outside it.
  4. THE BUDGET HAD COLLAPSED THE SECOND DECISION. The picture said "12 of 14 are now out of reach" after one shot; the simulation separately measured the budget costing 33 points of ceiling (78.8% unpriced against 46.0% priced). Two flat prices and two shots admit no middle. A drop is now charged FOR ITS LEVERAGE -- the closer it lands to the marked body the more it moves it and the more it costs -- which is the one pricing rule the physics supplies rather than a balance knob.

Also fixed from a failing gate: the target bearing was being drawn freely and often pointed where nothing travels, serving only 14 of 24 seeds. It is now snapped to a bearing the system actually travels along, WITH THE RADIUS LEFT ALONE -- the radius is what would have handed over the answer, and an earlier version of this oracle did exactly that and produced a "1.0 live moves" artifact that was nearly mistaken for a property of the game.

═══════════ STATED AGAINST MYSELF ═══════════

Four designs have now failed a pre-registered proof in this game: a single-shot aiming game, a sequencing game, and two policies for playing them. Across this increment three defects were in the measuring apparatus rather than the game -- an oracle arm that read exactly 100.0% because it was the ceiling measured against itself, a normalisation that would have hidden the very answer it was built to find, and a verdict line whose predicate contradicted its label, written in a script that did not use the instrument built one commit earlier to catch exactly that.

The project's standing tally, instrument defects outnumbering design findings roughly two to one, has not improved.

Also open and not hidden: the persona population has never been run against this ruleset, so the median-persona gate is unfired -- the ghost rule is demonstrably executable by A rule, not demonstrably by the median human. Multi-round play is unmeasured. No versus or co-op executor exists. Stages 1-5 of the Monte Carlo plan have not run.

═══════════ THE PROOF AGAINST THE SHIPPING MODULE, AFTER THOSE FIXES ═══════════

Re-measured against game/dark/steer.ts itself rather than a copy of its rules, 24 seeds:

  served by the viability oracle       22/24  (91.7%, up from 14/24)
  mean ceiling                         0.800
  RANDOM   share of ceiling            19.8%   negative control, priced
  BLIND    share of ceiling            19.1%   aim, watch, aim again
  GHOST    share of ceiling            81.2%   pick the dot nearest the ring, PRICED
  agency over doing nothing            0.800
  live sequences within 10% of ceiling 4.2 of 196
  price spread on a drop               0.6 to 1.5
  affordable actions at shot 2         12.5 of 14
  cost changes the best action          9.1%

  K1 policy reaches >=50% of ceiling            PASS
  K2 beats the blind rule by >=20 points        PASS
  K3 beats random by >=5x the noise floor       PASS
  K4 does NOT solve it (<=85% of ceiling)       PASS at 81.2%
  K5 >=70% of seeds served                      PASS
  K6 >=3 live sequences, not all of them        PASS
  K7 agency over doing nothing >=0.30           PASS
  K8 cost changes the best action on >=30%      FAIL at 9.1%
  K9 prices actually differ (spread >=0.4)      PASS
  K10 shot two has >=5 affordable actions       PASS at 12.5

NINE OF TEN, AND THE ONE FAILURE IS THE MIRROR OF THE DEFECT THE SCREENSHOT FOUND. The old budget was a wall; the new one is decoration. Too tight removes the second decision, too loose makes the price meaningless, and I have now sampled exactly two points on that dial in opposite ditches. Picking a third by hand and stopping when it passes would be tuning to the gate, so the dial is being swept and the curve reported -- including the possibility that NO value satisfies both, which would be a finding about the mechanic rather than a number to search harder for.

TWO THINGS I WOULD RATHER YOU SAW THAN MISSED. First, BLIND now reads 19.1% against RANDOM at 19.8%: the blind policy is WORSE than random, so the noise floor collapsed to 0.7 points and gate K3 passes trivially. It is a weak gate at these values and I am not claiming it as evidence. Second, the ceiling fell from 0.842 to 0.800 when the ring placement changed, so the 81.2% and the earlier 78.8% are shares of different denominators and are not directly comparable.

questions.text: Showing the player where every action lands is a large amount of information. The gate written to catch over-solving passed at 78.8% of the ceiling against a bar of 85%. Is that bar in the right place, or does a mechanic that takes a naive rule to four fifths of optimal play mean the game is now a lookup rather than a decision?

Pricing a mass drop by its LEVERAGE -- nearer the target body, stronger, dearer -- was chosen because the physics supplies it rather than because it balanced well. Is deriving a price from the mechanic's own physics genuinely more principled than tuning one, or does it just hide a tuned number behind a plausible story?

The screenshot and the simulation independently found the same defect (the budget collapsing the second decision) in the same increment. Does that convergence make the finding stronger, or does it mean one of the two instruments is redundant and I am paying twice for the same coverage?

The target ring is placed by snapping a seeded bearing to a direction the system travels, while leaving the radius alone. I claim this constrains difficulty without choosing the answer. What is the strongest argument that it still leaks the answer?

Four designs failed a pre-registered proof before this one. You gave a termination rule earlier -- stop when the skill gap does not move by more than the noise floor after an information mechanic is added. The gap moved from 16.3% to 78.8%. Does that discharge the rule, or is a design that needed four rebuilds evidence of something the rule does not capture?

The budget failed as a wall and then failed as decoration, and I am sweeping it rather than picking a third value. If no budget satisfies both 'the price changes the answer' and 'the second shot is still a choice', what does that tell you about a single-currency cost on a fourteen-action lattice -- and what would you put in its place?
